title: Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland
author: Lewis Carroll
setting: A riverbank on a hot afternoon, and the underground country Alice reaches by falling down a rabbit-hole
lengthNote: Twelve chapters, around 27,000 words — roughly twice the length of the manuscript it grew from
openingLine: Alice was beginning to get very tired of sitting by her sister on the bank, and of having nothing to do
summary: A child follows a rabbit underground and spends an afternoon among creatures who each treat a private rule as though it were the law. Alice grows, shrinks, is asked who she is by a caterpillar, and is sentenced before she is tried. The comedy is exact rather than woolly: almost every joke turns on someone taking a word at its face value, and the book ends when Alice stops agreeing to the fiction that the court is a court.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland
sourceText.note: A proofed transcription following Carroll’s revised wording. References give the chapter, which is the only division the book uses.

atAGlance.label: First told
atAGlance.note: On a boating excursion from Oxford with Robinson Duckworth and the three Liddell sisters.

atAGlance.label: Manuscript
atAGlance.note: Written out and illustrated by Carroll himself and given to Alice Liddell in November 1864.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: The 1865 printing was withdrawn after Tenniel objected to the reproduction of his pictures; the replacement is dated 1866.

atAGlance.label: Illustrator
atAGlance.note: Forty-two wood-engraved illustrations, made from Tenniel’s drawings by the Dalziel brothers.

structure.label: Chapters I–II
structure.title: A fall, and a body that will not hold still
structure.summary: Boredom, not magic, starts the book: Alice follows the Rabbit because an afternoon with nothing in it has become unbearable. Underground she finds a door she cannot fit, a bottle and a cake that change her size, and a pool made of her own crying. The problem is never the garden; it is that she cannot keep one body long enough to reach it.

scenes.title: Down the Rabbit-Hole
scenes.summary: The Rabbit’s waistcoat-pocket watch is the one detail Alice cannot explain away, and she is down the hole before she has thought about getting out.

scenes.title: The Pool of Tears
scenes.summary: Nine feet high and then two feet high, Alice tries lessons and recitation as proof of identity and finds both have gone wrong.

structure.label: Chapters III–IV
structure.title: Committees, and a house that does not fit
structure.summary: The soaked company invents a procedure for drying off in which everyone runs, everyone stops when told, and everyone wins. Then the Rabbit mistakes Alice for a servant, sends her for gloves, and she grows until she fills his house and has to be attacked from outside. Authority in Wonderland begins as a clerical error.

scenes.title: A Caucus-Race and a Long Tale
scenes.summary: The Mouse’s dry history fails to dry anybody; the Dodo’s race distributes prizes without a result.

scenes.title: The Rabbit Sends in a Little Bill
scenes.summary: Alice is taken for Mary Ann, grows to fill a house, and Bill the Lizard is sent down the chimney.

structure.label: Chapters V–VI
structure.title: Who are you, and what is a baby
structure.summary: The Caterpillar asks the question the first four chapters have made unanswerable, and gives Alice a mushroom that puts size under her own control at last. In the Duchess’s kitchen violence is ordinary household business, and the baby Alice rescues turns into a pig. The Cheshire Cat then explains, reasonably, that everybody present is mad.

scenes.title: Advice from a Caterpillar
scenes.summary: Alice recites ‘You are old, Father William’ wrongly and is told she is wrong; the mushroom becomes a tool rather than an accident.

scenes.title: Pig and Pepper
scenes.summary: Pepper, a flying frying-pan and a baby that becomes a pig; the Cat grins itself away and gives directions that depend on Alice not minding where she goes.

structure.label: Chapter VII
structure.title: A tea-party that cannot end
structure.summary: Time has stopped for the Hatter, so the party moves round the table instead of moving on. A riddle is asked and never answered, Alice is told she means the opposite of what she says, and the Dormouse tells a story about three sisters living in a treacle-well. It is the chapter in which conversation itself stops working.

scenes.title: A Mad Tea-Party
scenes.summary: No room at a table with room to spare; the raven and the writing-desk; the Hatter’s quarrel with Time; Alice walks out.

structure.label: Chapters VIII–X
structure.title: A queen who sentences instead of deciding
structure.summary: The garden is finally reached and turns out to be a croquet ground where the equipment is alive and the head gardeners are painting roses to cover a mistake. The Queen orders executions at the rate of about one a minute and nobody is ever executed. The Gryphon and the Mock Turtle then supply the book’s one sustained parody of school and sentiment.

scenes.title: The Queen’s Croquet-Ground
scenes.summary: Flamingo mallets and hedgehog balls; the Cat’s disembodied head raises the question of whether a head with no body can be beheaded.

scenes.title: The Mock Turtle’s Story
scenes.summary: The Duchess finds a moral in everything; the Mock Turtle grieves for a schooling built entirely of puns.

scenes.title: The Lobster Quadrille
scenes.summary: A dance, a recitation that goes wrong again, and Alice’s admission that she cannot go back to yesterday.

structure.label: Chapters XI–XII
structure.title: The trial, and the end of consent
structure.summary: Everything a court needs is present — judge, jury, witnesses, evidence, verdict — and every one of them is used in the wrong order. Alice grows through the proceedings as she loses patience with them, until she can call the court what it is made of. The waking on the bank does not cancel the dream; it returns the reader to a child who has learned to hear adult language differently.

scenes.title: Who Stole the Tarts?
scenes.summary: The Hatter gives evidence in terror, the jury writes down its own names in case it forgets them, and Alice begins to grow.

scenes.title: Alice’s Evidence
scenes.summary: A nonsense poem is read as proof, sentence is demanded before verdict, and Alice refuses the whole performance.

characters.name: Alice
characters.role: A child of about seven, underground for an afternoon
characters.summary: She is the only person in the book who revises her opinions. Alice tries school knowledge, polite introductions and recitation, notices each time that the method has failed, and keeps a running commentary on her own conduct that is often sharper than anything the creatures say to her.
characters.clue: She gives herself very good advice and seldom follows it, and she grows tall enough to stop being frightened of a court made of playing cards.

relationships.label: follows, and is mistaken for a servant by
sentenced by, and finally dismissive of

characters.name: The White Rabbit
characters.summary: He is the only creature in Wonderland who is frightened of being late, and the fear turns out to be well founded once the Queen appears. Anxious upwards and imperious downwards, he sets the plot going and then spends it running errands for people more dangerous than himself.
characters.clue: Pink eyes, a waistcoat-pocket watch, white kid gloves, and a permanent terror of the Duchess and of being late.

characters.name: The Mouse
characters.role: The first creature Alice tries to talk to
characters.summary: He is offended twice over by Alice’s cat and her neighbour’s terrier before he can begin his history, which is then delivered as the driest paragraph of Norman constitutional record Carroll could find. His long tale is the book’s first joke about a word doing two jobs at once.

characters.name: The Caterpillar
characters.role: Three inches high, on a mushroom, with a hookah
characters.summary: He conducts the only real interrogation in the book, and he is entitled to it: a creature that will shortly liquefy into a butterfly has a professional interest in whether anybody stays themselves. His contempt is useful to Alice, because it forces her to say out loud that she cannot explain herself.
characters.clue: Three inches high, smoking on a mushroom, and unimpressed by a girl who says she is not herself today.

characters.name: The Cheshire Cat
characters.role: A cat that can arrive and leave in pieces
characters.summary: The only creature who is candid with Alice, and the only one who can leave a conversation gradually. His directions are logically impeccable and practically useless, which makes him the book’s clearest demonstration that valid reasoning and helpful reasoning are different things.
characters.clue: It can vanish slowly from the tail upwards, leaving a smile behind, and it tells Alice that everyone present is mad, itself included.

characters.name: The Duchess
characters.role: A peeress with a kitchen full of pepper
characters.summary: In her own house she shakes a baby, sings about beating it, and is under sentence of execution; released, she becomes affectionate and turns every remark Alice makes into a moral. The two performances are the same person, which is the point: her manners have no connection to her conduct.

characters.name: The Hatter
characters.role: Host of a tea-party that never moves on
characters.summary: He quarrelled with Time while performing at a concert and has been stuck at six o’clock ever since, which turns his rudeness into a kind of grievance. He asks a riddle he cannot answer, corrects Alice’s grammar while ignoring her meaning, and later gives evidence in court shaking too hard to stand.
characters.clue: He fell out with Time at a concert and has been stuck at tea ever since, and he asks a riddle to which he admits he has not the slightest idea of the answer.

characters.name: The Queen of Hearts
characters.role: Sovereign of the croquet ground and the court
characters.summary: She has one procedure for every difficulty, and it is beheading. Nothing she orders is ever carried out, because the King quietly pardons everybody, so her power is pure noise — which is exactly what makes it frightening until somebody notices.
characters.clue: Her answer to every difficulty is the same three words, and the King pardons everyone behind her back so that none of her sentences is ever carried out.

characters.name: The Mock Turtle
characters.role: A grieving former pupil of the sea
characters.summary: He exists because mock turtle soup was made of veal, so Carroll gives him a calf’s head and a permanent sob. His account of an education in Reeling, Writhing and the different branches of Arithmetic is the book’s most sustained joke about school, and it is delivered as genuine grief.

themes.name: Identity and size
themes.summary: Alice’s height changes eleven times, and each change is treated as a question about who she is rather than how tall she is. Carroll keeps the enquiry in a child’s terms — other girls she knows, lessons she can or cannot recite — so that the philosophical problem arrives without any philosophical vocabulary.
themes.development: Panic in Chapter II, cross-examination in Chapter V, deliberate use of the mushroom afterwards, and finally a growth in Chapter XII that is an act of judgement rather than an accident.

themes.name: Rules and authority
themes.summary: Every creature Alice meets treats a private rule as universal and expects her to know it already. The book is unusually precise about how authority sounds: the Dodo’s procedure, the Queen’s sentences, the Hatter’s corrections and the King’s courtroom all use the grammar of settled law over nothing at all.
themes.development: A race with no contest, then a game with living equipment, then a trial that reverses verdict and sentence — the forms grow more official as they grow emptier.

themes.name: Language taken literally
themes.summary: Wonderland’s creatures are excellent close readers and terrible listeners. They hear the word and not the sentence, so ‘I mean what I say’ and ‘I say what I mean’ become different propositions, a tale becomes a tail, and a lesson is what lessens from day to day.
themes.development: The Mouse’s tale sets the pattern; the tea-party makes it a method; the trial turns it into a way of convicting somebody.

themes.name: Manners and violence
themes.summary: Politeness in Wonderland is not the opposite of cruelty but its packaging. A baby is shaken in time to a lullaby, a cook throws fire-irons during a conversation, and executions are ordered between croquet strokes, always in the correct register.
themes.development: Domestic in the Duchess’s kitchen, ceremonial on the croquet ground, and judicial by the trial, with the violence growing more formal as it grows less real.

themes.name: Lessons and what is remembered
themes.summary: Alice keeps reaching for the schoolroom to prove she is still herself, and the schoolroom keeps letting her down: multiplication that will not reach twenty, geography with the capitals in the wrong countries, poems that come out as other poems. Learning by heart is shown to be exactly that — learning that is not knowledge.
themes.development: Recitation fails in Chapter II, fails again under the Caterpillar in Chapter V, and is mourned in the Mock Turtle’s account of his education.

themes.name: The dream and the waking
themes.summary: The frame is not a get-out. Carroll lets the dream be dangerous while it lasts and then hands it to Alice’s sister, who dreams it again knowingly, so the book ends by describing the act of rereading rather than dismissing what was read.
themes.development: The fall, the afternoon underground, and a waking in which the cards become leaves and the Queen’s shrieks become a shepherd boy’s voice.

techniques.name: Nonsense logic
techniques.definition: Reasoning that is formally valid but proceeds from premises nobody has agreed to.
techniques.inThisBook: The Cat’s proof that it is mad, and its directions to Alice, are both watertight; the trouble is entirely with the starting point.

techniques.name: Parody
techniques.definition: Reproducing the shape of a known text while emptying or reversing its content.
techniques.inThisBook: Alice’s recitations deform improving verse into crocodiles and lobsters, and the joke works even for readers who no longer know the originals, because the failure is Alice’s memory rather than the poem.

techniques.name: Puns and literalism
techniques.definition: Treating a word’s other sense, or its plainest sense, as the one that was meant.
techniques.inThisBook: A long tale becomes a long tail, a school tortoise taught us, and ‘take more’ is answered with the impossibility of taking more than nothing.

techniques.name: Free indirect thought
techniques.definition: Narration that carries a character’s own phrasing without announcing it as speech.
techniques.inThisBook: Alice’s judgements leak into the narrator’s sentences — the ‘poor little thing’ who sits down and cries is being pitied by the narrator and by herself at the same moment.

techniques.name: Dream frame
techniques.definition: A narrative enclosed by a falling asleep and a waking.
techniques.inThisBook: The frame is used to end the book rather than to explain it: the sister’s second dream repeats Wonderland deliberately, which is not what waking up from a nightmare normally does.

techniques.name: Comic repetition
techniques.definition: A phrase or event repeated until the repetition itself becomes the joke.
techniques.inThisBook: ‘Down, down, down’, the Queen’s standing order for beheadings and the Dormouse’s treacle all work by recurrence rather than by any single funny line.

quotations.text: “and what is the use of a book,” thought Alice “without pictures or conversations?”
quotations.context: The second sentence of the book, as Alice looks over her sister’s shoulder.
quotations.analysis: Carroll puts a judgement about books at the front of a book, and the judgement is a child’s test of quality: pictures and conversations. What follows is made almost entirely of both, so the opening is a specification that the rest of the text meets exactly.

quotations.text: “Do cats eat bats? Do cats eat bats?” and sometimes, “Do bats eat cats?”
quotations.context: Falling down the rabbit-hole, growing sleepy.
quotations.analysis: The question reverses because Alice is going to sleep, and the reversal is the first sign that Wonderland runs on grammar rather than on events. She herself supplies the reason it does not matter which way round it is put — she cannot answer either — which is the exact logic the Hatter will later use against her.

quotations.text: “Curiouser and curiouser!” cried Alice (she was so much surprised, that for the moment she quite forgot how to speak good English)
quotations.context: Immediately after eating the cake, as she shoots up to nine feet.
quotations.analysis: Alice knows the comparative is wrong and says so in the same breath, so the nonsense is not outside language but one step past its usual limit. The doubling also gives the sentence an upward motion that matches what her body is doing, which is why no other word would serve.

quotations.text: But if I’m not the same, the next question is, Who in the world am I? Ah, that’s the great puzzle!
quotations.context: Alone in the hall, fanning herself with the Rabbit’s fan.
quotations.analysis: The reasoning is a syllogism: if I am not the same, then I am someone else, so which one? Alice tests it against the only evidence a child has — Ada’s ringlets, Mabel’s ignorance, the multiplication table — and the test fails on all three, which is why the chapter ends with her in a pool of her own tears.

quotations.text: “Speak English!” said the Eaglet. “I don’t know the meaning of half those long words, and, what’s more, I don’t believe you do either!”
quotations.context: Interrupting the Dodo’s proposal for a Caucus-race.
quotations.analysis: The Eaglet does what nobody else in the book will do: it demands that an official voice be translated. Carroll gives the demand to the smallest bird present and immediately undercuts it — the Eaglet hides a smile — so the challenge to pompous language is itself a piece of social manoeuvring.

quotations.text: At last the Dodo said, “everybody has won, and all must have prizes.”
quotations.context: Ending the Caucus-race, in which the runners began when they liked and stopped when the Dodo said so.
quotations.analysis: A result is announced for a contest that had no start, no course and no finish. The sentence is perfectly formed and entirely empty, and it is the first of several occasions on which Wonderland uses correct official phrasing to settle something that was never in dispute.

quotations.text: “Who are you?” said the Caterpillar.
quotations.context: The Caterpillar’s first words, spoken from the mushroom.
quotations.analysis: Four words, and the book has spent four chapters making them unanswerable. Coming from a creature about to dissolve into a chrysalis and re-form as something else, the question is also a professional one, which is why Alice’s complaint about changing size gets so little sympathy.

quotations.text: “I can’t explain myself, I’m afraid, sir,” said Alice, “because I’m not myself, you see.”
quotations.context: Answering the Caterpillar’s demand that she explain herself.
quotations.analysis: ‘Explain myself’ is a dead metaphor that Alice revives by taking it at full strength: to explain herself she would have to have a self to explain. The politeness of the phrasing — ‘I’m afraid, sir’ — keeps a genuinely frightening admission inside the manners of a well-brought-up child.

quotations.text: “Oh, you can’t help that,” said the Cat: “we’re all mad here. I’m mad. You’re mad.”
quotations.context: The Cheshire Cat, in a tree, after Alice objects that she does not want to go among mad people.
quotations.analysis: The Cat includes itself and Alice in the same sentence, which converts an insult into a description of the premises. It then offers a proof by comparison with a dog, and the proof is formally respectable: the only thing wrong with it is that the premises about dogs are invented.

quotations.text: “That depends a good deal on where you want to get to,” said the Cat.
quotations.context: Answering Alice’s request for directions from the fork in the wood.
quotations.analysis: The Cat gives the only genuinely sound advice in the book, and it is useless to Alice because she has no destination. The exchange quietly names the book’s method: nothing underground can be navigated by a traveller who has not decided what she wants.

quotations.text: “Well! I’ve often seen a cat without a grin,” thought Alice; “but a grin without a cat! It’s the most curious thing I ever saw in my life!”
quotations.context: Watching the Cat vanish slowly, ending with the smile.
quotations.analysis: Alice separates a property from the thing that has it and notices that the result is impossible rather than merely odd. Her method here is the book’s in miniature: she states the ordinary case first, then the departure from it, and treats the gap as evidence worth recording.

quotations.text: “No room! No room!” they cried out when they saw Alice coming. “There’s plenty of room!” said Alice indignantly
quotations.context: Arriving at the tea-party, where three creatures are crowded into one corner of a large table.
quotations.analysis: The lie is contradicted by the furniture in the same sentence, and Alice answers it with a fact rather than an argument. Carroll establishes in two lines that this table runs on assertion, which is why the riddle that follows is allowed to have no answer.

quotations.text: The Hatter opened his eyes very wide on hearing this; but all he said was, “Why is a raven like a writing-desk?”
quotations.context: The Hatter’s first remark to Alice, dropped into a conversation about hair-cutting.
quotations.analysis: A riddle is a contract: you ask, I try, you tell me. The Hatter breaks it at every stage, and when Alice asks for the answer he says he has not the slightest idea. The joke is not the raven; it is a form of words that keeps its shape after its purpose has been removed.

quotations.text: “I’ve had nothing yet,” Alice replied in an offended tone, “so I can’t take more.”
quotations.context: The March Hare has just invited her to take more tea.
quotations.analysis: Alice is right and is told she is wrong, and the correction — that you cannot take less than nothing — is true of arithmetic and false of tea. It is the clearest case in the book of a creature winning an argument by changing which system the words belong to.

quotations.text: the Queen was in a furious passion, and went stamping about, and shouting “Off with his head!” or “Off with her head!” about once in a minute.
quotations.context: During the croquet game, in which the hoops keep walking away.
quotations.analysis: Carroll gives the rate rather than the drama: about once a minute. Turning a death sentence into a statistic drains it of menace, and the reader learns before Alice does that these orders are noise — the King has been quietly pardoning everybody behind the Queen’s back.

quotations.text: “We called him Tortoise because he taught us,” said the Mock Turtle angrily: “really you are very dull!”
quotations.context: Explaining why the old Turtle who taught him was called Tortoise.
quotations.analysis: The pun is delivered angrily, as though Alice were the slow one, and that is what makes the scene work: in Wonderland the person who has to have the joke explained is always at fault. The Mock Turtle’s whole education runs on the same principle, which is why he mourns it.

quotations.text: ‘Take care of the sense, and the sounds will take care of themselves.’
quotations.context: One of the Duchess’s morals, delivered with her chin in Alice’s shoulder.
quotations.analysis: The Duchess has inverted the proverb about pounds and pence, and the inversion is a fair description of Carroll’s own practice: mind the meaning and the sound follows. Coming from a woman who finds a moral in everything and observes none of them, it is advice the book both offers and mistrusts.

quotations.text: “I could tell you my adventures⁠—beginning from this morning,” said Alice a little timidly: “but it’s no use going back to yesterday, because I was a different person then.”
quotations.context: Offering to tell the Gryphon and the Mock Turtle her adventures.
quotations.analysis: This is the same question the Caterpillar asked, answered at last — not by working out who she is, but by accepting that yesterday’s Alice is no longer available for comparison. Her timidity over saying it is the measure of how large the admission is.

quotations.text: “Begin at the beginning,” the King said gravely, “and go on till you come to the end: then stop.”
quotations.context: Instructing the White Rabbit to read the verses offered as evidence.
quotations.analysis: The King’s only contribution to jurisprudence is a rule about reading aloud, delivered gravely as though it settled something. It is also the book’s sole piece of usable advice, and Carroll gives it to the least competent person in the room.

quotations.text: “No, no!” said the Queen. “Sentence first⁠—verdict afterwards.”
quotations.context: The Queen’s response to the King’s call for the jury to consider its verdict.
quotations.analysis: Every element of due process is present in the trial and only the order has gone; the Queen’s correction is procedural rather than mad. Alice’s reply, that the idea is stuff and nonsense, is the first time she names the problem instead of arguing inside it.

quotations.text: “Who cares for you?” said Alice, (she had grown to her full size by this time.) “You’re nothing but a pack of cards!”
quotations.context: The end of the trial, with Alice grown back to her full size.
quotations.analysis: ‘Nothing but’ does the work: the court is reduced to the material it is made of. Alice had noticed as much in Chapter VIII and kept it to herself; saying it aloud is what ends the dream, because the cards have no power once nobody agrees to treat them as a court.

timeline.label: Charles Lutwidge Dodgson born at Daresbury in Cheshire
timeline.detail: The eldest son of a clergyman, and the third of eleven children.

timeline.label: Dodgson is appointed Mathematical Lecturer at Christ Church, Oxford
timeline.detail: He held the post for a quarter of a century and lived in college for the rest of his life.

timeline.label: The river excursion of 4 July
timeline.detail: Dodgson tells the first version of the story to the three Liddell sisters on a boat trip towards Godstow.

timeline.label: Alice’s Adventures Under Ground given to Alice Liddell
timeline.detail: Written out and illustrated by Dodgson himself; the published book more than doubles it.

timeline.label: The first printing is withdrawn
timeline.detail: Tenniel objected to the quality of the reproduction of his illustrations.

timeline.label: The replacement impression reaches readers
timeline.detail: Dated 1866, this is the effective first published edition.

timeline.label: Through the Looking-Glass appears
timeline.detail: Published in December and dated 1872, again with Tenniel’s illustrations.

timeline.label: The Nursery ‘Alice’
timeline.detail: Carroll’s own shortened version for very young children, with coloured plates.

timeline.label: The last substantial revision of the text
timeline.detail: New settings incorporate Carroll’s final corrections to the standard wording.

timeline.label: Carroll dies at Guildford
timeline.detail: He died in January at his sisters’ house, The Chestnuts.

timeline.label: The book comes out of copyright in Britain
timeline.detail: New illustrated editions follow at once, among them Arthur Rackham’s.

timeline.label: The Under Ground manuscript comes to the British Museum
timeline.detail: Bought by American subscribers and presented to Britain; it is now British Library Add MS 46700.

timeline.label: Disney’s animated Alice in Wonderland
timeline.detail: It folds material from Through the Looking-Glass into Wonderland and fixes the book’s popular image for a century.

places.name: Christ Church, Oxford
places.note: Dodgson’s college for the whole of his adult life, and the Liddells’ home in the Deanery.

places.name: Folly Bridge, Oxford
places.note: Where the boat was hired for the excursion of 4 July 1862.

places.name: Godstow
places.note: The upstream destination of that afternoon’s row, where the party took tea on the bank.

places.name: Daresbury, Cheshire
places.note: Carroll’s birthplace, and the county that supplies the Cheshire Cat’s grin.

places.name: Guildford
places.note: The Chestnuts, his sisters’ house, where he died in January 1898.

criticalViews.position: A book about logic and language
criticalViews.summary: Carroll taught mathematics and wrote on logic, and this reading takes the creatures’ arguments seriously as arguments: most are valid, and the fault lies in the premises or in a shift between senses of a word.
criticalViews.counter: It can make Wonderland sound like a textbook, when a great deal of the book’s force is emotional — fear of being someone else, and the misery of being talked down to.

criticalViews.position: A child’s book that satirises adult institutions
criticalViews.summary: School, etiquette, committees, monarchy and the law all appear in forms a child can follow, and all fail their own tests. On this account Alice is learning to tell a rule that helps people live together from a rule that only protects whoever is shouting.
criticalViews.counter: Carroll disliked being told what his book meant, and a satirical target can usually be swapped for another without the scene changing at all.

criticalViews.summary: Because the 1864 manuscript survives, Wonderland can be read against the shorter story Carroll first wrote out, and the most famous episodes — the tea-party, the Cheshire Cat, the Duchess’s kitchen — turn out to be additions made for a public rather than for one child.
criticalViews.counter: Treating the manuscript as the ‘real’ version mistakes a private gift for a draft; the two texts were made for different readers and do different work.

essayQuestions.question: How does Carroll use changes of size to explore who Alice is?
essayQuestions.focus: Identity, the body and the limits of self-knowledge
plan: Establish the pattern: eleven changes of height, each of them answered with a question about identity rather than about measurement.
Read Chapter II closely — Ada’s ringlets, Mabel’s ignorance, the multiplication table — as an attempt to prove identity from evidence.
Set the Caterpillar’s interrogation against that failure, and note that Alice’s answer is an admission rather than a solution.
Turn the argument at the mushroom: from Chapter V onwards size is a tool she uses, not an accident she suffers.
Close on Chapter XII, where growing large is an act of judgement about the court rather than a physical event.

essayQuestions.question: ‘Wonderland is not lawless; it is over-governed.’ Discuss.
plan: Distinguish the two claims: disorder, or an excess of rules that nobody has agreed to.
Use the Caucus-race as the first case — a complete procedure with no contest inside it.
Read the croquet ground for the relation between ceremony and effect: sentences are passed about once a minute and nothing is carried out.
Examine the trial for order rather than content: judge, jury, evidence and verdict are all present and only the sequence has gone.
Decide what Alice’s final refusal shows — that authority here depends on the consent of everybody who agrees to be frightened.

essayQuestions.question: What does Carroll do with parody, and does it still work for a reader who does not know the originals?
plan: Set out what is being parodied: improving verse of the kind children were made to learn by heart.
Show how the parodies are staged as failures of memory, not as literary jokes — Alice sets out to recite and something else comes out.
Compare the Mock Turtle’s account of his schooling, where the joke is on the curriculum rather than on any one poem.
Test the question directly: what survives for a reader with no original in mind, and what is lost.
Conclude on what recitation is for in the book — a proof of identity that keeps failing.

essayQuestions.question: How does the dream frame affect the way the book ends?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure, the waking and the sister’s second dream
plan: Describe the frame precisely: a drowsy afternoon, a fall, and a waking with leaves on the face.
Ask whether the dream is used to explain the impossibilities, and note how little of the book depends on their being explained.
Read the transformations at the waking — cards into leaves, shrieks into a shepherd boy — as a translation rather than a cancellation.
Examine the sister’s deliberate re-dreaming, and what it says about rereading a book you already know.
Weigh the ending against the fear the middle chapters generate: is the frame a comfort, or an admission that none was needed?

discussionQuestions: Alice is the only character in the book who changes her mind. Does that make her the heroine, or just the outsider?
The Queen orders constant executions and none takes place. Is she frightening?
Almost every creature corrects Alice’s English. Why does Carroll make rudeness so specifically grammatical?
The tea-party has no plot and no consequence. What would the book lose without it?
Tenniel’s pictures arrived with the first published text. Can the book now be read without them?

related.why: Another traveller who measures an impossible country deadpan, and another book that children were given after the satire had been trimmed off it.
Talking animals with settled manners — the opposite arrangement, where the creatures are courteous and the rules hold.
Children left to work out an adult world for themselves, without any of Wonderland’s licence to be rude back.
Another heroine who talks herself through trouble, and another book in which recitation is a test of who a child is.
Nonsense logic promoted to social weapon: characters who reason impeccably from premises they have just invented.
